2026-11-10-body-02.description:
In a vacuum you don't explode, because your tissue is strong enough. Water boils at body temperature, so wet spots like your eyes and mouth go first, and NASA astronaut-physician Michael Barratt puts useful consciousness at about 12 seconds. In December 1966, NASA test subject Jim LeBlanc's suit hose came loose in a Houston vacuum chamber. He felt his saliva boil off his tongue before passing out, and the chamber was repressurized. He had no long-term effects.

2026-11-10-body-03.description:
A hiccup is a spasm of your diaphragm, the muscle below your lungs, followed by your vocal cords snapping shut: that's the "hic". Most bouts last a few minutes; hiccups lasting more than 48 hours are called persistent, and Cleveland Clinic and the NHS say to see a doctor if they go past two days. Experts haven't found a proven hiccup cure. Charles Osborne started hiccuping after a fall while hanging a hog in 1922 and didn't stop until 1990: 20 to 40 times a minute, an estimated 430 million hiccups. He married twice and had eight children.

2026-11-10-body-04.title: What Happens When You Get Brain Freeze?
2026-11-10-body-04.pinned_comment: What gives you the worst brain freeze: ice cream, a slushie, or ice water? Did the tongue trick work for you?

2026-11-10-body-04.topic_source: backlog #1: mandatory next_topic_must_be, promised by the hiccups video (2026-11-10-body-3) with 'and the tongue trick that helps it thaw' (paid off in lines 12-14: press your tongue to the roof of your mouth)
2026-11-10-body-04.description:
Brain freeze (scientific name: sphenopalatine ganglioneuralgia) starts when something cold, like ice cream, suddenly chills the roof of your mouth. Your body tries to warm up: blood vessels in your head change size to let in extra blood, and the trigeminal nerve, which carries pain from your face, sends the signal. You feel it in your forehead and temples instead of your mouth. It's not serious and usually lasts a few seconds to two minutes. To help it pass, press your tongue or thumb against the roof of your mouth, or sip something warm or room temperature.

2026-11-10-body-05.topic_source: backlog #1: mandatory next_topic_must_be, promised by the brain freeze video (2026-11-10-body-4) with 'the same reaction that puffs up a hissing cat' (paid off in line 6: 'That's how a hissing cat puffs up to look bigger.')
2026-11-10-body-05.description:
Goosebumps (piloerection) are an automatic reaction of your sympathetic nervous system, your fight-or-flight mode. Tiny muscles at the base of each hair follicle (the arrector pili) contract, so the hairs stand up and small bumps form. Cold, fear, shock, excitement and even music or a movie can set them off. In animals it makes them look bigger, like a cat that puffs up while it hisses; in humans it mostly helps conserve a little heat. A 2020 Harvard study in mice suggests a second job: the same nerve, bridged by that muscle, wakes up hair follicle stem cells, and mice kept in the cold grew new hair in under two weeks.

2026-11-10-body-06.description:
That "asleep" feeling is temporary paresthesia: sitting with your legs crossed too long puts sustained pressure on a nerve (body position can also limit blood flow), so the messages between your foot and your brain get interrupted and the foot goes numb. Move, the pressure is released, and the nerve "wakes up": that's the pins and needles, a tingling, prickling or burning feeling that fades in a minute or two with no permanent damage. If it won't go away or happens often, see a doctor.

2026-11-10-body-07.description:
A knocked-out adult tooth put back in its socket, or stored properly, within five minutes will likely survive. Hold it by the crown, never the root: the root carries tiny fibers it needs to heal. Don't scrub it or put it in water. If it won't go back in, keep it in milk or your own saliva and get to a dentist or emergency department right away. Baby teeth are not put back.

2026-11-10-body-08.description:
A narrow passage called the eustachian tube links each middle ear to the back of your nose and throat. It stays shut until you swallow, yawn or chew; then it opens, air gets in, and the pressure on both sides of your eardrum evens out. On a plane the pressure can change faster than the tube can adjust, so hearing goes muffled. If ear discomfort, fullness or muffled hearing lasts more than a few days, or is severe, see a doctor.

2026-11-14-body-01.description:
A charley horse is a muscle cramp: a sudden tightening, most often in the calf, where the muscle contracts on its own and can't relax. It can last from a few seconds to 10 minutes, and most people get them at night or while resting. Stretching and massaging the muscle, or putting your weight on that leg, may ease it, and the muscle can stay sore afterward. See a doctor if cramps happen often, are severe, or come with swelling or numbness.
